evidence.quote: SR 85 heads north from the border as a two-lane road, passing through the Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument.

evidence.claim: South of Why, State Route 85 crosses Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument on two lanes before reaching the Mexican border at Lukeville.
evidence.quote: The southern terminus of SR 85 is located at the Mexican border near Lukeville in Pima County. From Lukeville to Why, SR 85 is designated the Organ Pipe Cactus Parkway by ADOT.

evidence.claim: South of Why, State Route 85 crosses Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument on two lanes before reaching the Mexican border at Lukeville.
evidence.quote: SR 85 heads north from the border as a two-lane road, passing through the Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument.

evidence.claim: The monument’s landscape includes volcanic mountains, washes and broad valleys.
evidence.quote: volcanic layered mountains, ribbons of washes and expansive valleys

evidence.claim: Arizona designated a 21-mile segment as the Organ Pipe Cactus Parkway in 2008; ADOT identifies the desert vegetation and scenery as the reasons for that recognition.
evidence.quote: In 2008, a 21-mile segment of SR 85 was designated the Organ Pipe Cactus Parkway in recognition of its extraordinary desert vegetation and scenery as it passes through Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument.

evidence.claim: The monument is also an International Biosphere Reserve. Human life in this Sonoran Desert landscape extends back thousands of years, alongside its communities of plants and animals.
evidence.quote: The sights and sounds of Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, an International Biosphere Reserve, reveal a thriving community of plants and animals. Human stories echo throughout the Sonoran Desert, chronicling thousands of years of desert living.

evidence.claim: The larger highway corridor developed in connection with Ajo’s copper industry.
evidence.quote: The oldest and historic portions of route are the southern segments south of Gila Bend, associated with the rich copper mines at Ajo.

evidence.claim: Maricopa and Pima counties graded the road from Gila Bend to the junction that became Why, and SR 85 entered the state highway system in 1936.
evidence.quote: Maricopa and Pima Counties graded and improved their segments of future SR 85 from Gila Bend all the way to what would become the “wye” junction of future SR 85 and SR 86, named Why in 1930. In 1936, the Arizona Highway Department added SR 85 to the state highway system.

evidence.claim: After the monument’s establishment in 1937, paving reached from Why to Lukeville in 1942 and 1943. That southern road became part of SR 85 in 1955.
evidence.quote: The final segment between the Why and the International Border at Lukeville was paved in 1942 and 1943, although it was not considered a portion of SR 85 until 1955.

evidence.claim: After the monument’s establishment in 1937, paving reached from Why to Lukeville in 1942 and 1943. That southern road became part of SR 85 in 1955.
evidence.quote: In 1937, President Franklin D. Roosevelt established Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument

evidence.claim: Begin at Why’s junction with SR 86 and follow SR 85 south into the monument.
evidence.quote: The highway leaves the monument boundary and heads to a junction with SR 86 in Why.

evidence.claim: At the Kris Eggle Visitor Center, a short nature trail introduces desert plants and rare Quitobaquito pupfish.
evidence.quote: Take a leisurely walk on the 1/10-mile accessible nature trail that starts at the visitor center and enjoy seeing rare Quitobaquito pupfish, an abundance of cacti and desert plants

evidence.claim: Lukeville marks the highway’s southern end; beyond the border, the road continues into Sonoyta as Mexican Federal Highway 8.
evidence.quote: The road continues across the border into Mexico to the town of Sonoyta as Mexican Federal Highway 8.

evidence.claim: Why’s name outlasted the road junction that supplied it.
evidence.quote: The town derives its name from the two major highways, State Routes 85 and 86, that once intersected in a Y-intersection.

evidence.claim: State Routes 85 and 86 once met in a Y shape here; ADOT later replaced that junction with a conventional intersection farther south for traffic safety.
evidence.quote: The Arizona Department of Transportation (ADOT) later eliminated the old Y-intersection for traffic safety and made a conventional intersection south of the original.

evidence.claim: State Routes 85 and 86 once met in a Y shape here; ADOT later replaced that junction with a conventional intersection farther south for traffic safety.
evidence.quote: The town derives its name from the two major highways, State Routes 85 and 86, that once intersected in a Y-intersection.

evidence.claim: The community lies north of Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, near the western edge of the Tohono Oʼodham Indian Reservation.
evidence.quote: It lies near the western border of the Tohono Oʼodham Indian Reservation and due north of Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument

evidence.claim: The junction divides three onward routes: SR 86 runs east toward Tucson, SR 85 northwest toward Ajo, and SR 85 south through the monument to Lukeville.
evidence.quote: SR 86 heads east from this junction towards Tucson and southeastern Arizona. SR 85 heads northwest from this junction to the town of Ajo.

evidence.claim: The junction divides three onward routes: SR 86 runs east toward Tucson, SR 85 northwest toward Ajo, and SR 85 south through the monument to Lukeville.
evidence.quote: SR 85 heads north from the border as a two-lane road, passing through the Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument. The highway leaves the monument boundary and heads to a junction with SR 86 in Why.

evidence.claim: Why lies ten miles south of Ajo, at this junction of the two state highways.
evidence.quote: 10 miles (16 km) south of Ajo, Arizona.

evidence.claim: The visitor center’s tenth-mile nature trail includes rare Quitobaquito pupfish alongside cacti and other desert plants.
evidence.quote: Take a leisurely walk on the 1/10-mile accessible nature trail that starts at the visitor center and enjoy seeing rare Quitobaquito pupfish, an abundance of cacti and desert plants

evidence.claim: An exhibit room introduces the monument, which was set aside in 1937 as an example of the Sonoran Desert.
evidence.quote: Visit the Kris Eggle Visitor Center, browse the bookstore, and explore the exhibit room to learn why this area is so special.

evidence.claim: An exhibit room introduces the monument, which was set aside in 1937 as an example of the Sonoran Desert.
evidence.quote: Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument was set aside on April 3rd, 1937 for future generations as an exemplar of the Sonoran Desert.

evidence.claim: The organ pipe cactus has several upright stems rising from a short trunk near ground level.
evidence.quote: This cactus species has several narrow stems that rise vertically, growing from a single short trunk just above the ground level.

evidence.claim: It grows predominantly on rocky hillsides and is sensitive to frost, making it rarer in low desert areas where frost is more frequent.
evidence.quote: The plant is predominantly found on rocky hillsides up to 900 m (3,000 ft) in elevation.  It is sensitive to frost, so the species is rare in low desert areas, which can be more susceptible to frost.

evidence.claim: The cactus’s English name comes from its resemblance to a pipe organ; its stems seldom branch, instead extending from their tips.
evidence.quote: Its English common name is derived from its resemblance to a pipe organ.

evidence.claim: The cactus’s English name comes from its resemblance to a pipe organ; its stems seldom branch, instead extending from their tips.
evidence.quote: These stems rarely branch but rather grow annually from the tip of the last growth.

evidence.claim: Lukeville is a border town entirely within Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument.
evidence.quote: It is the terminus of State Route 85 and is located entirely within Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument.

evidence.claim: Lukeville is a border town entirely within Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument.
evidence.quote: Lukeville is a small unincorporated town on the Mexico–United States border

evidence.claim: Charles Luke, brother of World War I aviator Frank Luke, started the community.
evidence.quote: It was started by Charles Luke, brother of World War I aviator Frank Luke

evidence.claim: An executive order established its port of entry in 1949, primarily for passenger vehicles and pedestrians.
evidence.quote: The Lukeville, Arizona Port of Entry was established by Executive Order in 1949. It has primarily been a port of entry for passenger vehicles and pedestrians.

evidence.claim: The road connects Arizona’s SR 85 with Mexican Federal Highway 8 in Sonoyta.
evidence.quote: It connects Mexican Federal Highway 8 in Sonoyta, Sonora, with Arizona State Route 85, in Lukeville, Arizona.

evidence.claim: In 2011, modifications funded by the Federal Highway Administration and Mexican businesses provided for truck inspections and improved traffic flow.
evidence.quote: Modifications made using funding from the Federal Highway Administration and Mexican businesses in 2011 facilitate the inspection of trucks and improve general throughput.

evidence.claim: Much of the crossing’s traffic heads for the beach town of Puerto Peñasco in Sonora, linking the desert highway to a destination beyond the border.
evidence.quote: Much of the traffic using this crossing is people traveling to the popular beach town of Puerto Peñasco, Sonora.
